questions.q: For a chemical reaction, half-life period $\left(\mathrm{t}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is 10 minutes. How much reactant will be left after 20 minutes if one starts with 100 moles of reactant and the order of the reaction be (i) zero, (ii) one and (iii) two?
questions.solution:
For zero order, $k=\frac{x}{t}\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{t}_{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{\mathrm{a}}{2 \mathrm{~K}} \\
& 10=\frac{100}{2 \times \mathrm{K}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~K}=5 \\
& 5=\frac{\mathrm{x}}{20} \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=100 \therefore(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{x})=0
\end{aligned}$

For 1st order, No. of half lives $=\frac{20}{10}=2\therefore(a-x)=\frac{100}{2^2}=25$

For 2nd order, $\mathrm{k}=\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{at}(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{x})}\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \mathrm{t}_{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{ak}} \\
& 10=\frac{1}{100 \times \mathrm{k}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}=10^{-3} \\
& \therefore 10^{-3}=\frac{\mathrm{x}}{100 \times 20 \times(100-\mathrm{x})} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=66.66 \\
& \therefore(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{x})=33.33
\end{aligned}$

options: $f(x)$ is continuous but not differentiable at $x=\frac{1}{2}$

questions.solution:
The absolute value function can be rewritten as a piecewise function:
\(f(x)= \begin{cases}1-2 x, & \text { if } x \leq \frac{1}{2} \\ -(1-2 x), & \text { if } x \gt \frac{1}{2}\end{cases}\)
2. Check for continuity at \(x=\frac{1}{2}\) :
Left-hand limit: \(\lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}}(1-2 x)=1-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=0\)
Right-hand limit: \(\lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}}-(1-2 x)=-\left(1-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)=0\)
Function value: \(f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\left|1-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right|=|1-1|=0\)
Since the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value are all equal, the function is continuous at \(x=\frac{1}{2}\).
3. Check for differentiability at \(x=\frac{1}{2}\) :
Left-hand derivative: \(f^{\prime}(x)=-2\) for \(x\lt \frac{1}{2}\), so \(\lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}} f^{\prime}(x)=-2\).
Right-hand derivative: \(f^{\prime}(x)=2\) for \(x \gt \frac{1}{2}\), so \(\lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}^{+}} f^{\prime}(x)=2\).
Since the left-hand derivative and right-hand derivative are not equal, the function is not differentiable at \(x=\frac{1}{2}\).

options: none of $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ is divisible by $(x-1)$
$g(x)$ is divisible by $(x-1)$ but $f(x)$ is not divisible by $(x-1)$
$f(x)$ is divisible by $(x-1)$ but $g(x)$ is not divisible by $(x-1)$
questions.solution:
$\because$ By remainder theorom
$\begin{aligned}
& \phi(\omega)=0 \quad \& \phi\left(\omega^2\right)=0 \quad\left(\omega, \omega^2 \text { are complex cube root of unity }\right) \\
& \Rightarrow f(1)+\omega g(1)=0 \quad \& \quad f(1)+\omega^2 g(1)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow f(1)=g(1)=0 \\
& \therefore \phi(1)=f(1)+g(1)=0
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $a, b, c$ are in A.P. and if the equations $(b-c) x^2+(c-a) x+(a-b)=0$ and $2(c+a) x^2+(b+c) x=0$ have a common root, then
questions.solution:
Given:
- \(a, b, c\) are in A.P. \(\Rightarrow b=\frac{a+c}{2}\)
- Two quadratic equations have a common root:
\(\begin{array}{l}
(b-c) x^2+(c-a) x+(a-b)=0 ... (1) \\
2(c+a) x^2+(b+c) x=0 ... (2) 
\end{array}\)
Step-by-step approach:
Let the common root be \(\alpha\). Then it satisfies both:
From (2):
\(2(c+a) \alpha^2+(b+c) \alpha=0 \Rightarrow \alpha(2(c+a) \alpha+b+c)=0\)
So either \(\alpha=0\) or \(2(c+a) \alpha+b+c=0\)
Check both cases:
Case 1: \(\alpha=0\)
Put in (1):
\((b-c)(0)^2+(c-a)(0)+(a-b)=a-b \neq 0(\text { since } a \neq b) \Rightarrow \text { Not a root }\)
Case 2:
\(2(c+a) \alpha+b+c=0 \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{-(b+c)}{2(c+a)}\)
Substitute into equation (1), solve, and simplify using \(b=\frac{a+c}{2}\)
Eventually, this leads to:
\(a^2+c^2=2 b^2 \Rightarrow a^2, c^2, b^2 \text { are in A.P. }\)

questions.q: The straight line $\frac{x-3}{3}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{0}$ is
questions.solution:
The given equation of the straight line is:
\((x-3) / 3=(y-2) / 1=(z-1) / 0\)
The direction ratios of this line are 3,1, and 0. A line parallel to the \(z\)-axis has direction ratios 0,0, and 1.
If the dot product of the direction ratios of two lines is zero, then the lines are perpendicular.
Let's check the dot product of the direction ratios of the given line and a line parallel to the z-axis:
\(\left(3^* 0\right)+(1 * 0)+(0 * 1)=0\)
Since the dot product is zero, the given line is perpendicular to the z-axis.
Therefore, the correct answer is (4).
